Ancient Artefacts Associated with Geographical Representations

Prehistory to the pre-modern era

A chronological survey of material, non-paper artefacts that encode geographic or spatial knowledge — from a 25,000-year-old engraved mammoth tusk to a 16th-century Inca relief stone. Every entry is drawn from and cross-checked against The History of Cartography reference series (University of Chicago Press) or an equivalent primary/institutional source; citations are given under each object. This is a private preview shared with newsletter subscribers ahead of publication — please don’t share the link further.

c. 25,000 BCE Europe — Czech Republic

Pavlov mammoth-tusk map

Found 1962 · Moravia

Excavated by Czech archaeologist Bohuslav Klíma, who directed digs at Pavlov I (1952–1972), a Gravettian hunter-gatherer camp.

Engraved mammoth ivory. Klíma read the geometric pattern as a schematic map of the surrounding hills — the meandering Dyje river, the Pálava slopes, and the camp itself at center.

Photos: museum display (full object) and detail of the engraved pattern.

c. 10,000 BCE (est.) North America — United States

Map Rock (Celebration Park)

Snake River, Canyon County, Idaho

HOC gives no date for the petroglyph itself; the c. 10,000 BCE figure is a popularly circulated estimate from Idaho tourism sources (Canyon County, Visit Idaho), not from an archaeological survey or dating study — treat as approximate and unverified. It also sits in tension with local attribution of the site to the (much more recent) Northern Shoshone.

Basalt boulder petroglyph described as “one of the more convincing examples of a map in rock art,” interpreted as a map of the Snake River drainage system near Givens Hot Springs, Idaho. Confirmed in The History of Cartography, Vol. 2, Bk. 3, Ch. 4 (Lewis), p. 64, fig. 4.6, photo by G. Malcolm Lewis, by permission of the Idaho Historical Society. The image shown here is a different photo of the same boulder.

Image note: photo courtesy of Canyon County, Idaho (canyoncounty.id.gov) — not a Creative Commons or public-domain release; used here with attribution pending confirmation of reuse terms.

c. 5000–4000 BCE Middle East — Iraq

Tepe Gawra landscape vase

Excavated 1927–1938

University of Pennsylvania Museum expedition, directed by E. A. Speiser and later C. Bache. Vase from Level XII, Room 206.

Painted ceramic vase, 12 panels — 10 geometric, 2 depicting landscape scenes (“the landscape jar”). Confirmed in The History of Cartography, Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Delano Smith), p. 72, figs. 4.15–4.16. Original photograph: Arthur J. Tobler, Excavations at Tepe Gawra, vol. 2 (University of Pennsylvania Press, 1950), pl. LXXVIIIa; by permission of the Iraq Museum, Baghdad.

Image note: the image shown here is an AI-generated redrawing based on a photograph of the vase, not the original Tobler/Iraq Museum photograph itself.

c. 3700–3000 BCE Caucasus — Russia

Maikop Vase

Excavated 1895 · Adygea, North Caucasus

Excavated by Russian archaeologist Nikolai Veselovsky, opening the Maikop kurgan burial mound; now in the Hermitage Museum.

Silver vessel from an elite Bronze Age burial, engraved with a landscape frieze of hills, a tree, and animals (goats, deer). Confirmed in The History of Cartography, Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Delano Smith), p. 72, fig. 4.18, dated there “ca. 3000 BCE.”

Image note: AI-generated redrawing based on a photograph published in Blagoje Govedarica, “Majkopska gravura” [The Maikop Engraving], Godišnjak Centra za balkanološka ispitivanja (Yearbook of the Centre for Balkan Studies), vol. 41 (2012), 37–42, fig. 3 — not the original photograph itself.

c. 3600–3200 BCE Europe — Malta

Ħaġar Qim terracotta model

Malta (National Museum of Archaeology, Valletta) · Ġgantija phase

Two fragments survive of a larger original.

A modeled foundation slab bearing the lower courses of what have been interpreted as the walls and jambs of a five-apsed temple — possibly a demonstration model or three-dimensional reference plan used during actual construction. Confirmed in The History of Cartography, Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Delano Smith), p. 81.

Image note: AI-generated redrawing based on a photograph published in Isabelle Vella Gregory, “Immensity and Miniaturism: The Interplay of Scale and Sensory Experience in the Late Neolithic of the Maltese Islands,” Oxford Journal of Archaeology, vol. 35 (2016), 329–344, fig. 4(c) (photo: Daniel Cilia / Heritage Malta) — not the original photograph itself.

c. 3000–2500 BCE Europe — Malta

Tarxien limestone sculpture

Malta (National Museum of Archaeology, Valletta)

Found in a temple built at Tarxien late in the Neolithic period.

Sculptured limestone block interpreted by some archaeologists as a detailed plan representation of a building with rectangular living spaces. Confirmed in The History of Cartography, Vol. 1, Ch. 4 (Delano Smith), p. 81, fig. 4.31.

Image note: AI-generated redrawing based on a photograph published in Isabelle Vella Gregory, “Immensity and Miniaturism: The Interplay of Scale and Sensory Experience in the Late Neolithic of the Maltese Islands,” Oxford Journal of Archaeology, vol. 35 (2016), 329–344, fig. 4(d) (photo: Daniel Cilia / Heritage Malta) — not the original photograph itself.

c. 2300 BCE–1000 CE East & Inner Asia — Russia

Boyarskaya pisanitsa

Khakassia

No single named discoverer identified; documented through Soviet- and post-Soviet-era archaeological survey.

Petroglyphs depicting yurt-like settlement structures, livestock and food preparation.

Wikimedia Commons

ca. 1500 BCE Middle East — Iraq

Plan of Nippur

Excavated 1889–1900

University of Pennsylvania expedition, directed by John Punnett Peters with John Henry Haynes as field director; tablet published by Hermann Hilprecht in 1903.

Cuneiform clay tablet town plan — possibly the earliest town plan drawn to scale — showing the temple of Enlil in its enclosure, city walls, canals, storehouses, and a park. Confirmed in The History of Cartography, Vol. 1, Ch. 6, fig. 6.7.

Wikimedia Commons — Public Domain

c. 1500–200 BCE Europe — Italy

Bedolina Map

Studied from the 1950s · Val Camonica, Lombardy

Italian archaeologist Emmanuel Anati, who founded the Centro Camuno di Studi Preistorici (1964) and called this panel “the oldest geographical map found in Europe.”

Depicts cultivated fields, paths and irrigation channels.

Photo: Luca Giarelli, Wikimedia Commons

c. 1500–200 BCE Africa — Namibia

Southern African rock engravings (Maggs corpus)

Documented from 1960 · Twyfelfontein

Ernst Rudolf Scherz documented 2,500+ engravings from 1960 (published 1975), building on Tim Maggs’ analysis of the site’s cartographic content.

Engravings of animal tracks and routes clustered near natural water sources — read by Maggs as encoding paths and the locations of waterholes across the surrounding terrain.

Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA

c. 1500–500 BCE East & Inner Asia — Mongolia

Grave plans from Ich-Tengerin-Am

Mongolia

Date range is a scholarly estimate for the region’s Bronze Age petroglyph tradition, not stated precisely in the source.

Rectangular grid/lattice petroglyphs, described erroneously by Okladnikov (1972) as Bronze Age rectangular courts or yards (“hose”), but consistent with other Mongolian examples recognized as representations of graves. Confirmed in The History of Cartography, Vol. 2, Bk. 2, Ch. 1 (Delano Smith), p. 9, fig. 1.8, after E. A. Novgorodova, Alte Kunst der Mongolei, trans. Lisa Schirmer (Leipzig: E. A. Seemann, 1980), fig. 72.

Image note: AI-generated redrawing based on the photograph in Novgorodova, Alte Kunst der Mongolei (1980), fig. 72, as reproduced in The History of Cartography, Vol. 2, Bk. 2, Ch. 1, fig. 1.8 — not the original photograph itself.

ca. 600 BCE Middle East — Iraq

The Babylonian World Map

Excavated by Hormuzd Rassam at Sippar · acquired by the British Museum, 1882

Largest dimensions of the original: 12.5 × 8 cm.

Clay tablet showing the relationship between legendary regions beyond the ocean and the Babylonian world. Parallel lines running to and from Babylon (the elongated rectangle) represent the Euphrates, while a circular band represents the salt sea. Confirmed in The History of Cartography, Vol. 1, Ch. 6, fig. 6.10.

By permission of the Trustees of the British Museum, London (BM 92687).

c. 203–211 CE Europe — Italy

Forma Urbis Romae

Fragments rediscovered 1562, relocated to the Capitoline Museums 1673 · Rome

Antiquarian sculptor Giovanni Antonio Dosio excavated the first fragments near Santi Cosma e Damiano, under Torquato Conti; over a thousand further fragments recovered since.

Marble map of ancient Rome at 1:240 scale, originally displayed in the Temple of Peace. This fragment shows the seating plan of the Theater of Pompey (“THEATRVM”).

Image note: AI-generated redrawing based on a reconstruction illustration by Ulysses K. Vestal, theaterofpompey.com (copyrighted free use), via Wikimedia Commons — not a photograph of the original marble.

1136–1137 CE East & Inner Asia — China

Yu ji tu stele

Xi’an, Stele Forest/Beilin Museum

No single “discovery” — a continuously known public monument.

Engraved stone map of Song-dynasty China, gridded at a 100-li scale.

Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

c. 1400–1533 CE South America — Peru

Sayhuite Stone

Near Cuzco

No single discovery — a long-known Inca site.

Granite monolith carved with terraces, channels and over 200 figures, widely interpreted as a three-dimensional relief map of Tahuantinsuyu (the Inca empire) — though the reading is contested; alternative interpretations include a ceremonial model or a hydraulic scale model.

Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA
